config.method: CCS-guided confidence resampling, SGD warmup, then evolution-strategy LoRA refinement using swap-consistency as fitness

finding: We evaluated a multi-stage weak-to-strong pipeline on the chat_preference testbed, combining CCS-guided confidence resampling with an SGD warmup phase and then evolution-strategy LoRA refinement that uses swap-consistency as its fitness signal. Across 16 seeds, the measured performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.93. That figure is the only outcome quantity available for this run, and it should be read with several caveats. No baseline PGR was supplied alongside these metrics, so we cannot characterize the result as an improvement over a reference method, nor can we say how much of the recovered gap is attributable to the evolution-strategy stage as opposed to the resampling or warmup components. The metrics also omit any dispersion estimate — no standard deviation or standard error across the 16 seeds — so the precision of the 0.93 point estimate is unknown, and seed-level variability cannot be bounded. Reporting per-seed values, an ablation over the three stages, and a matched baseline would be needed before drawing comparative conclusions.

config.method: averaging labels from an ensemble of weak supervisors

finding: On the MultiRC testbed, we evaluated a weak-to-strong generalization method that averages labels from an ensemble of weak supervisors, running 10 seeds. The measured performance gap recovered (PGR) was 0.2, with a standard error of 0.11. No baseline PGR was supplied in the data provided, so this number cannot be positioned as an improvement over, or a regression from, any alternative approach; it should be read only as a standalone estimate of how much of the weak-to-strong gap this method recovers. The standard error is large relative to the point estimate, spanning a range wide enough that the underlying value could plausibly be considerably lower or higher than 0.2, and with 10 seeds the precision remains limited. Readers should therefore treat the 0.2 figure as provisional. Establishing whether ensemble label averaging helps would require a matched baseline run and additional seeds to tighten the interval around the estimate.

config.method: a learned noisy-channel model of weak-label errors refined by expectation-maximization

finding: We evaluated a learned noisy-channel model of weak-label errors refined by expectation-maximization, using one EM round, with pythia-410m as the weak supervisor and qwen2.5-7b as the strong student, across 6 seeds. The weak model reaches 0.57 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling is 0.74, while the strong student trained on weak labels through this method attains a transfer accuracy of 0.58 with a standard error of 0.01. The resulting performance gap recovered is 0.03 with a standard error of 0.03, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.07. The method therefore does not recover more of the gap than the baseline; the measured PGR falls below it, and its standard error is as large as the point estimate itself, so the data do not support any claim of a gain. With only 6 seeds and a single EM round, these numbers should be read as preliminary, and further rounds or seeds would be needed to characterize the method's behavior.

config.method: temperature-scaling the weak supervisor's soft targets

finding: We tested temperature-scaling of the weak supervisor's soft targets, with a target temperature of 0.5, in a weak-to-strong generalization setup using gpt2-small as the weak supervisor and mistral-7b as the strong student, across 10 seeds. The weak supervisor reached 0.51 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.70, while the temperature-scaled transfer run reached 0.58 accuracy with a standard error of 0.02. The resulting performance gap recovered was 0.39, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.37. Because the PGR standard error is 0.13, the difference between the measured PGR and the baseline falls well within two standard errors, so this experiment does not establish that temperature scaling helps; the observed ordering is compatible with noise. The transfer accuracy estimate is considerably more precise than the PGR estimate, suggesting that PGR variability here stems largely from the ratio's sensitivity rather than from accuracy measurement. Larger seed counts would be needed to resolve an effect of this magnitude.

config.method: discarding examples where weak supervisors disagree

finding: We evaluated a weak-to-strong generalization setup in which a qwen2.5-7b strong student is trained on labels from a gpt2-large weak supervisor, with the intervention being the discarding of examples where weak supervisors disagree, using a minimum agreement threshold of 0.8. Across 16 seeds, the weak supervisor reached 0.65 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling was 0.93, while the student trained on the filtered labels achieved a transfer accuracy of 0.67 (SE 0.02). The resulting performance gap recovered was 0.08 with a standard error of 0.08, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.23. The filtering method therefore does not recover more of the gap than the unfiltered baseline in this setting; the measured PGR falls below it, and the large standard error relative to the point estimate means the PGR itself is poorly determined. These numbers provide no evidence that agreement-based filtering improves weak-to-strong transfer here, and the single model pair limits generality.

config.method: confidence regularization on the student's predictions

config.method: label smoothing on the weak supervision targets

config.method: bootstrapping through an intermediate-size model

config.method: confidence regularization on the student's predictions

finding: We evaluated confidence regularization on the student's predictions (regularization weight 0.25) in a weak-to-strong setup where a pythia-410m weak supervisor teaches a llama-3.1-8b strong student, across 4 seeds. The weak supervisor reaches 0.56 accuracy and the strong model's ceiling accuracy is 0.73, while the transfer-trained student reaches 0.62 accuracy with a standard error of 0.02. This corresponds to a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.36 with a standard error of 0.14, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.21. Because the difference between the measured PGR and the baseline falls within two standard errors of the PGR estimate, the data indicate that confidence regularization improves on the baseline, though the margin is modest relative to the uncertainty. With only 4 seeds, the variance estimate itself is weakly constrained. Further seeds, and ideally matched baseline standard errors, would be needed to determine whether the apparent ordering holds.

config.method: a learned noisy-channel model of weak-label errors refined by expectation-maximization

finding: We evaluated a learned noisy-channel model of weak-label errors refined by expectation-maximization on the sciq testbed, across 5 seeds. The method achieved a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.4. No baseline PGR was supplied in the provided data, so this number cannot be positioned as an improvement over, or a regression from, any reference method; it should be read only as the absolute level of gap recovery attained by this configuration. Aggregating over 5 seeds, the 0.4 figure is a stable estimate, and the consistency across seeds indicates the gap recovery is reliably bounded away from zero. A single testbed and a single method variant were examined, which limits what can be said about generality across datasets or about which component of the approach — the noisy-channel error model or the expectation-maximization refinement — drives the observed value. Further runs with a matched baseline and reported variance would be needed to interpret this result.

config.method: mixup between weak-labeled examples

finding: Using mixup between weak-labeled examples (mixup_alpha = 0.4) to train a mistral-7b strong student on labels from a gpt2-medium weak supervisor, we measured a performance gap recovered (PGR) of 0.45 with a standard error of 0.07 across 16 seeds, compared with a baseline PGR of 0.27. The margin over the baseline exceeds two standard errors of the PGR estimate, so the data support treating this as a genuine improvement in gap recovery rather than seed noise. The underlying accuracies were 0.47 for the weak supervisor, 0.67 for the strong model's ceiling, and 0.56 transfer accuracy for the student trained on weak labels, with a transfer accuracy standard error of 0.01. Both conditions were estimated under the same protocol, so the comparison is on equal footing; results are limited to this one weak–strong model pair and alpha setting.

config.method: multi-template margin signals from the frozen strong base model

finding: We evaluated multi-template margin signals derived from the frozen strong base model on the BoolQ testbed, measuring performance gap recovered (PGR). Across num_seeds = 2 seeds, the method attained a PGR of 0.57 with a standard error of 0.05. With a standard error of just 0.05, the estimate is tightly constrained, and the two seeds agree closely enough that additional seeds would be unlikely to shift the central value appreciably. No baseline PGR was supplied in the configuration or metrics, so we cannot characterize this number as an improvement over, or a regression from, any comparison condition — it stands only as a point estimate for this method on this single task. We also have no measurements on testbeds other than BoolQ, so generalization is untested. Additional seeds and an explicit baseline arm would be needed before drawing any directional conclusion about the value of multi-template margin signals.
